title: An MLP learns a sequence of useful coordinate systems
summary: See how nonlinear hidden layers turn a linear classifier into a more expressive function.

sections.title: A linear boundary has a limited vocabulary
paragraphs: A perceptron combines inputs with weights and a bias, then applies a decision rule. Its boundary is a hyperplane, which works only when one linear separation describes the task. An MLP introduces hidden layers that transform the representation before the final decision. The hidden features can make a difficult boundary in the original coordinates simpler in the learned coordinates, while still being trained from a single output objective.

sections.title: Nonlinearity is what prevents collapse
paragraphs: Consider h = ReLU(xW₁ + b₁) followed by y = hW₂ + b₂. If the ReLU were removed, the two affine maps would combine into one affine map, regardless of hidden width. With ReLU, different input regions activate different hidden units, yielding different local linear behaviors. For input width 4, hidden width 8, and output width 3, the model has 4·8 + 8 + 8·3 + 3 = 67 parameters.
sections.formula: h = φ(xW₁ + b₁);  y = hW₂ + b₂

sections.title: Expressiveness is only one requirement
paragraphs: An MLP can represent complicated functions, but representation capacity does not ensure successful optimization or good generalization. Too little width may underfit; excessive capacity can memorize limited data. Scale input features, inspect hidden activations, and first fit a tiny synthetic task with a known boundary. The XOR problem is useful because a single linear boundary fails, while a small nonlinear hidden representation can separate its four points.

exercise.prompt: Why do three linear layers without any nonlinear activation still represent only one affine transformation? Include the role of biases.
exercise.answer: Substituting each layer into the next multiplies the weight matrices and combines the transformed biases into one final bias. The result is xW + b for some W and b. Extra depth alone introduces no nonlinear decision boundary.

takeaways: Hidden layers learn representations for later decisions.
Without nonlinearities, stacked affine layers remain affine.

title: Backpropagation reuses local derivatives efficiently
summary: Derive the backward pass of a small network and understand why shared paths require accumulation.

sections.title: Start from the quantity you want to improve
paragraphs: Backpropagation begins with a scalar loss and asks how each intermediate value affected it. Each operation receives an upstream sensitivity and sends sensitivities to its inputs using its local derivative. Reusing intermediate results makes this efficient even when many parameters influence the loss. The algorithm computes derivatives; the optimizer is a separate component that decides how to use them to change the parameters.

sections.title: Differentiate a two-layer network
paragraphs: For Z = XW₁ + b₁, H = ReLU(Z), and Y = HW₂ + b₂, let G be the gradient of loss with respect to Y. Then the gradient for W₂ is HᵀG, while the gradient for H is GW₂ᵀ. Multiply that by the indicator Z > 0 to obtain the gradient for Z. The first weight gradient is Xᵀ times that result. Bias gradients sum over every batch position where the bias was reused.

sections.title: Test sharing and reductions deliberately
paragraphs: A parameter used twice must receive both contributions. Similarly, changing a loss from a sum to a mean changes all gradients by the reduction factor. Use a tiny float64 network and compare a few analytical entries against finite differences. Avoid checking exactly at a ReLU kink, where the classical derivative is undefined. If gradients disagree, inspect axis sums and transposes before blaming numerical precision or the framework.

exercise.prompt: A scalar weight w appears in y = wx + wz, and the upstream gradient ∂L/∂y is g. What is ∂L/∂w, and why is one contribution insufficient?
exercise.answer: The gradient is g(x + z). The shared weight affects y through both products, so reverse-mode differentiation sums gx and gz. Keeping only one path would optimize a different function from the one used in the forward pass.

takeaways: Backpropagation and optimization are separate operations.
Shared parameters and broadcast biases accumulate contributions.

title: Activations control which signals and gradients pass through
summary: Compare ReLU, GELU, and SiLU by their response to negative inputs and their derivatives.

sections.title: A gate changes the local computation
paragraphs: Without an activation, a layer only changes coordinates linearly. An activation makes its response depend on the current input. ReLU keeps positive values and clips negative ones to zero. GELU and SiLU use smooth, input-dependent weighting instead of a hard cutoff. All three are applied elementwise, so the tensor shape stays unchanged even though the represented function becomes nonlinear.

sections.title: Compare the formulas on one axis
paragraphs: ReLU(x) = max(0, x). GELU(x) = xΦ(x), with Φ the standard normal cumulative distribution function. SiLU(x) = xσ(x), using the logistic sigmoid. For a large positive input, each behaves approximately like the identity. For moderately negative inputs, GELU and SiLU can produce small negative outputs, while ReLU produces zero. Their smoothness changes gradient behavior, but does not by itself establish which activation will work best for a particular architecture.
sections.formula: ReLU(x) = max(0, x);  GELU(x) = xΦ(x);  SiLU(x) = x/(1 + e⁻ˣ)

sections.title: Inspect distributions, not just names
paragraphs: A ReLU unit receiving only negative preactivations can stop receiving useful gradient through that gate. Changing an activation can also alter activation variance, so initialization and learning rate should be reconsidered when making an architectural comparison. Plot outputs and derivatives over a small interval, then inspect layerwise activation histograms during training. Treat a better final score as an empirical result under a specified setup, rather than proof that smoothness always improves learning.

exercise.prompt: For inputs [−2, 0, 3], what are the ReLU outputs? At which input is its ordinary derivative undefined, and what derivative is commonly selected there in implementations?
exercise.answer: The outputs are [0, 0, 3]. The ordinary derivative is undefined at zero because the one-sided slopes differ. Implementations commonly select zero there as a valid subgradient convention.

takeaways: Activations change local signal and gradient flow.
Activation choice interacts with initialization and data scale.

title: A loss function defines what counts as a mistake
summary: Relate squared error and cross-entropy to target types, likelihood assumptions, and reduction choices.

sections.title: The output must match the question
paragraphs: Regression asks for numerical values; classification asks for a distribution over alternatives. Mean squared error penalizes the squared distance between prediction and target, making large residuals disproportionately influential. Cross-entropy penalizes low probability assigned to the observed class. Choosing between them is therefore more than choosing a convenient API: it defines the statistical assumptions and error preferences of the task.

sections.title: Connect gradients to prediction errors
paragraphs: For squared error (ŷ − y)²/2, the derivative with respect to ŷ is simply ŷ − y. For softmax cross-entropy, the gradient with respect to a logit is predicted probability minus the target probability. This compact result explains why confidently wrong predictions produce strong corrective signals. In practice, a numerically stable cross-entropy implementation accepts logits and combines log-softmax with the negative log-likelihood calculation.

sections.title: Reduction and masking belong to the definition
paragraphs: A summed loss grows with batch size or sequence length, while a mean depends on what positions enter its denominator. Padding and ignored labels must be excluded consistently. Applying softmax before a loss that expects logits changes its input semantics and can weaken learning. For regression with heavy-tailed noise, squared error may be dominated by a few outliers; consider whether that sensitivity matches the application before treating it as an optimizer problem.

exercise.prompt: A classifier assigns probabilities [0.1, 0.7, 0.2], and the true class is the third. What is the cross-entropy gradient with respect to its three logits?
exercise.answer: Subtract the one-hot target [0, 0, 1] from the prediction: [0.1, 0.7, −0.8]. Gradient descent lowers the first two logits and raises the third, moving probability toward the observed class.

takeaways: Match loss semantics to the target and output representation.
Specify the averaging denominator and ignored positions.

title: Initialization sets the scale of both activations and gradients
summary: Understand Xavier and Kaiming initialization as attempts to keep signals usable through depth.

sections.title: Depth repeatedly multiplies random quantities
paragraphs: Before learning begins, each layer already transforms the magnitude of its inputs. If those magnitudes grow or shrink systematically, a deep network can start with saturated activations, tiny gradients, or enormous outputs. Initialization aims to place the model in a regime where information and gradients can travel through many layers. It does not solve optimization completely, but it prevents avoidable scale problems before the first update.

sections.title: Count incoming contributions
paragraphs: A preactivation sums fan_in weighted inputs. Under simplifying independence and zero-mean assumptions, its variance scales roughly with fan_in times weight variance times input variance. Xavier initialization balances incoming and outgoing widths, often using variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out). Kaiming initialization accounts for rectification and commonly uses variance 2/fan_in for ReLU forward signal preservation. The chosen mode and activation gain matter; these are not interchangeable names for arbitrary small random weights.

sections.title: Symmetry and orientation can break the setup
paragraphs: Initializing every hidden unit identically can keep their updates identical, preventing useful specialization. Randomness breaks that symmetry. Matrix orientation matters too: a library may store a linear weight as [out, in] even when the mathematical expression uses [in, out]. Check which axis a custom initializer treats as fan_in. Inspect activation and gradient scales across several layers on a fixed batch; gross trends can reveal a mismatch before expensive training.

exercise.prompt: A ReLU layer has fan_in = 100. Using the common Kaiming forward-preserving rule, what weight variance and standard deviation should you expect?
exercise.answer: The variance is 2/100 = 0.02 and the standard deviation is √0.02 ≈ 0.1414. These values follow the stated assumptions and parameter orientation; they are not a universal prescription for every gated or residual architecture.

takeaways: Initialization is a signal-scale design choice.
Check fan definitions and activation gains in custom layers.

title: Normalization is defined by the axes it averages
summary: Compare BatchNorm, LayerNorm, and RMSNorm through their statistics and train-time behavior.

sections.title: Normalize a specified collection of values
paragraphs: Normalization rescales activations using statistics computed over particular axes. BatchNorm commonly shares statistics across examples and spatial positions for each channel. LayerNorm commonly computes statistics across features within one example or token. RMSNorm rescales using the root mean square without subtracting the mean. These distinctions determine whether one example's output depends on other examples in the batch and whether training and evaluation need different statistics.

sections.title: Write down the reduction dimensions
paragraphs: For a token vector x with d features, LayerNorm subtracts its feature mean and divides by the square root of feature variance plus epsilon, then applies learned affine parameters. RMSNorm uses sqrt(mean(x²) + epsilon) instead. For x = [2, 4], centering gives [−1, 1], whereas RMS scaling preserves both positive signs. Neither operation changes the number of features, but they remove or preserve different information.

sections.title: Mode changes and batch size matter
paragraphs: BatchNorm typically updates running statistics during training and uses them during evaluation. Tiny or unrepresentative batches can make those estimates unreliable. LayerNorm and RMSNorm generally use current per-example statistics in both modes, although other layers may still change behavior. Check normalized_shape carefully: normalizing tokens and features together is different from normalizing each token independently. Do not describe normalization as a guaranteed cure for instability; residual scale and optimizer settings still matter.

exercise.prompt: For an input [B, T, D], you want each token normalized across features without mixing examples or positions. Which axes should LayerNorm reduce, and what parameter shape is typical?
exercise.answer: Reduce only the final D axis, producing separate statistics for each of the B·T tokens. The learned scale and bias typically each have shape [D], shared across examples and positions.

takeaways: Reduction axes define normalization semantics.
RMSNorm rescales without subtracting the feature mean.

title: Residual connections let a block refine an existing representation
summary: Understand the identity path, gradient flow, and shape requirements behind skip connections.

sections.title: Learning a correction can be easier
paragraphs: A residual block outputs the input plus a learned transformation. If the transformation is initially small, the block begins near an identity map and can learn a useful correction. This gives a deep model a direct path for carrying existing information forward. The purpose is not to make every layer redundant; each branch can contribute a refinement while preserving a stable reference representation.

sections.title: The backward path includes an identity term
paragraphs: For y = x + F(x), the local Jacobian is I + J_F. The identity contribution provides a route for gradients that does not require multiplying only through the residual branch. Addition requires compatible shapes. If the number of features or spatial resolution changes, the shortcut may need a learned projection or another explicit transformation. That projected path is no longer an exact identity, so its initialization and dimensions deserve separate attention.

sections.title: Residuals do not make scale irrelevant
paragraphs: Repeatedly adding large branches can still cause activations to grow, especially in very deep networks. Normalization placement, initialization, and residual scaling remain important. Also distinguish addition from concatenation: concatenating a skip feature changes width and lets a later layer combine features, while addition mixes them immediately in shared coordinates. When a skip addition fails, inspect both shape and meaning rather than inserting a projection solely to silence the error.

exercise.prompt: A block receives [8, 64, 32, 32] images and its main branch outputs [8, 128, 16, 16]. Can you add the original input directly? Propose a compatible shortcut.
exercise.answer: No: channel count and spatial dimensions differ. A 1×1 convolution with 128 output channels and stride 2 can map the shortcut to [8, 128, 16, 16], provided the spatial sizing conventions match the main branch.

takeaways: An identity path supports information and gradient flow.
Residual additions require aligned shapes and feature meanings.

title: Dropout and weight decay regularize different parts of training
summary: Distinguish random activation removal from direct pressure on parameter magnitude.

sections.title: Two interventions, two mechanisms
paragraphs: Dropout injects noise into intermediate representations by randomly removing activations during training. This discourages the model from depending too heavily on particular co-activations. Weight decay shrinks parameters during optimization, influencing the solutions training favors. Both can reduce overfitting in suitable settings, but they act on different objects and need not provide the same benefit. Their strength should be selected using validation data.

sections.title: Preserve the expected activation scale
paragraphs: With inverted dropout and drop probability p, a retained activation is multiplied by 1/(1 − p). The expectation of the resulting activation equals the original value, so evaluation can use the unmodified activation without random masking. Weight decay applies a shrinkage proportional to the current weight. Under adaptive optimizers, decoupling this shrinkage from gradient normalization distinguishes AdamW from simply adding an L2 penalty to the loss.
sections.formula: Dropout(x) = m ⊙ x/(1 − p),  with mᵢ ∼ Bernoulli(1 − p)

sections.title: Use training mode deliberately
paragraphs: Forgetting to call eval() leaves dropout active and makes ordinary evaluation stochastic. Conversely, training in evaluation mode removes the intended regularization. Large dropout can underfit or damage information flow, especially when few features carry the signal. Decay policies often treat biases and normalization parameters differently, but the policy should be recorded rather than assumed. Compare training and validation curves together to distinguish useful regularization from merely making optimization harder.

exercise.prompt: With dropout probability 0.25, a scalar activation of 6 is either removed or rescaled. What value does it take when retained, and what is its expectation?
exercise.answer: When retained it becomes 6/0.75 = 8; otherwise it is zero. Its expectation is 0.75·8 + 0.25·0 = 6. This preserves the mean, although the sample-to-sample variance increases.

takeaways: Dropout perturbs activations; decay shrinks parameters.
Training and evaluation modes must match the intended behavior.

title: An embedding layer is a learned table of coordinates
summary: Connect token IDs, lookup operations, gradient updates, and the geometry of learned representations.

sections.title: An identifier is not a measurement
paragraphs: Token ID 900 is not semantically nine times token ID 100. IDs are arbitrary indices, so feeding their raw numerical values into a model imposes a false ordering and distance. An embedding table assigns each ID a learned vector. Training can then place useful distinctions in continuous coordinates without assuming that nearby integers represent related concepts.

sections.title: Lookup is equivalent to a sparse selection
paragraphs: For vocabulary size V and embedding width D, the table has shape [V, D]. IDs shaped [B, T] produce vectors [B, T, D]. Multiplying one-hot vectors by the table would yield the same result, but direct lookup avoids constructing huge one-hot arrays. In a pure lookup path, only selected rows receive gradient contributions from that batch; repeated IDs accumulate contributions. Tying this table to an output projection can introduce additional gradient paths.
sections.formula: E ∈ R^(V×D);  token IDs [B, T] → embeddings [B, T, D]

sections.title: Interpret geometry with care
paragraphs: Embedding similarity reflects the training objective and data, not an intrinsic definition of meaning. Two tokens used in similar contexts may become close even if they are opposites in a particular task. Padding rows need a deliberate treatment, and unknown-token behavior depends on the tokenizer. An embedding table also has substantial memory cost: a vocabulary of 50,000 and width 768 contains 38.4 million parameters before any attention layer is added.

exercise.prompt: An embedding table has 1,000 rows and width 32. A batch contains IDs [4, 4, 9]. How many rows are accessed, what output shape results, and what happens to repeated-ID gradients?
exercise.answer: Two distinct rows are accessed, but the output contains three vectors and has shape [3, 32]. Contributions from both occurrences of ID 4 are summed into the gradient for row 4 in the lookup path.

takeaways: Token IDs select learned vectors rather than encode numerical magnitude.
Embedding geometry depends on the training signal.

title: Convolution shares a local detector across space
summary: Derive convolution shapes and understand what pooling and stride discard.

sections.title: Images contain repeated local patterns
paragraphs: An edge can appear in many image locations. A convolution applies the same small filter across positions, reusing parameters and building in a preference for local patterns. Compared with a fully connected layer on every pixel, this dramatically reduces the number of independent weights. Deeper layers combine local responses into larger receptive fields, although a large theoretical receptive field does not mean every distant pixel contributes equally in practice.

sections.title: Track channels and spatial dimensions
paragraphs: A standard 2D convolution with C_in input channels, C_out output channels, and a k×k kernel uses C_out·C_in·k² weights, plus biases if enabled. For one spatial axis, output size is floor((n + 2p − d(k − 1) − 1)/s + 1), with padding p, dilation d, and stride s. A 3×3 stride-2 layer with padding 1 maps a 32-pixel axis to 16.

sections.title: Downsampling trades detail for efficiency
paragraphs: Pooling summarizes neighborhoods, while strided convolution learns how to combine and downsample them. Both can lose small structures or introduce sensitivity to alignment. Weight sharing gives convolution a form of translation equivariance under suitable boundary conditions; it does not make an entire network perfectly translation-invariant. Check padding, stride, and pooling when diagnosing shifted-image failures. Use a tiny image with one marked pixel to trace which output locations respond.

exercise.prompt: A convolution takes 3 input channels to 16 output channels using 3×3 kernels and one bias per output channel. How many parameters does it have? Does image size change that count?
exercise.answer: There are 16·3·3·3 = 432 weights and 16 biases, totaling 448 parameters. Image height and width change computation and activation storage, but not this layer's parameter count.

takeaways: Convolution shares local weights across spatial positions.
Stride and pooling save computation by discarding spatial detail.

title: Recurrent networks summarize a sequence one step at a time
summary: Compare vanilla recurrence with the controlled memory updates of LSTMs and GRUs.

sections.title: A hidden state carries the past
paragraphs: An RNN updates a state as each token arrives, reusing the same transition parameters across time. This supports variable-length sequences and naturally fits streaming input. The state must compress information from earlier observations into a fixed-width representation, creating a trade-off between compact memory and preserving details that may only become relevant later. Sequential dependence also limits parallelism across time during ordinary recurrent computation.

sections.title: Gates control writing and retention
paragraphs: A vanilla recurrence might use h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t−1) + b). Its long-range gradients involve repeated Jacobian products, which can shrink or grow rapidly. LSTMs introduce a cell state with gates controlling retention, writing, and exposure. GRUs use update and reset gates with a more compact state arrangement. Gates make memory flow learnable, but do not guarantee perfect retention over arbitrarily long sequences.
sections.formula: h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t−1) + b)

sections.title: Sequence boundaries are part of the model
paragraphs: Reset hidden state between unrelated examples unless the task intentionally treats them as one stream. When training long streams with truncated backpropagation, detach state at planned boundaries to limit graph length while retaining its numerical value. Padding and sequence lengths must prevent artificial tokens from corrupting the meaningful final state. Compare recurrent models and attention models under matched data and latency constraints rather than treating one historical architecture as universally obsolete.

exercise.prompt: You process a long stream in chunks and carry the final hidden state into the next chunk. What does detaching that state change, and what information does it preserve?
exercise.answer: Detaching preserves the hidden state's numerical summary for the next forward computation, but stops gradients from crossing into the previous chunk. This limits backpropagation length and memory use while retaining forward-time recurrence.

takeaways: Recurrent state compresses earlier observations.
Gates improve memory control but do not eliminate long-range optimization issues.

title: Schedules, warmup, and clipping control the update scale
summary: Distinguish planned learning-rate changes from emergency limits on gradient magnitude.

sections.title: An effective step size changes over training
paragraphs: Early training, representation formation, and late refinement may benefit from different update magnitudes. A learning-rate schedule specifies how the optimizer's base step size changes with progress. Warmup gradually increases that rate at the beginning. Gradient clipping instead reacts to the current gradient, preventing an unusually large norm from producing an excessive update. These mechanisms address different situations and should be recorded separately.

sections.title: Separate a schedule from a direction
paragraphs: A linear warmup reaches the target learning rate after a chosen number of steps. A cosine decay then lowers it smoothly toward a minimum over the remaining budget. Global-norm clipping rescales the entire gradient vector only when its norm exceeds a threshold, preserving direction. Elementwise clipping has different geometry because it can change relative coordinate sizes. With mixed precision, clipping must inspect unscaled gradients.

sections.title: Count the unit your schedule uses
paragraphs: A schedule defined over optimizer steps should not advance on every microbatch during gradient accumulation. Resuming a checkpoint must restore the schedule position, and changing total steps changes the meaning of a cosine schedule. Log both learning rate and gradient norm so that a loss spike can be linked to a concrete event. Constant severe clipping may hide instability rather than solve it; inspect loss scaling, data outliers, and the optimizer configuration.

exercise.prompt: A gradient vector is [3, 4] and the global-norm threshold is 2. What clipped vector results? Would clipping each coordinate to [−2, 2] produce the same direction?
exercise.answer: Its norm is 5, so global clipping scales it by 2/5, giving [1.2, 1.6]. Elementwise clipping gives [2, 2], which changes the direction. The two procedures are not interchangeable.

takeaways: Scheduling changes the planned step size.
Global-norm clipping preserves direction while limiting magnitude.
